written.myAnswer: ASCII encodes text characters as binary codes so computers can store and process text.
ASCII represents a limited character set, mainly English characters; Unicode can represent characters from many languages and writing systems.
Unicode assigns each character a unique code point, enabling characters from many languages to be represented.
A common method is two’s complement: write the positive value in binary, invert its bits, and add 1.
Unsigned integers use all their bits for zero and positive values, so they have a greater positive range than same-size signed integers.
More bits allow more distinct integer values. For an unsigned n-bit integer, the range is 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
Unsigned integers represent zero and positive values without allocating values to negative numbers, making them suitable for non-negative quantities.
Single precision has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. Its approximate range is 1.4 × 10⁻⁴⁵ to 3.4 × 10³⁸.
Floating-point numbers have limited precision and range. Rounding errors, overflow, or underflow can therefore affect scientific results.
Unicode assigns code points to characters; for example, A is U+0041, ا is U+0627, and ब is U+092C.
Integers are stored as binary bit patterns. Unsigned integers use all bits for non-negative values, while signed integers commonly use two’s complement to represent positive and negative values.
For positive integers, repeated division by 2 gives 13₁₀ = 1101₂, and positional place values give 1101₂ = 13₁₀. For 4-bit two’s complement, −5₁₀ = 1011₂, and 1011₂ represents −5₁₀.
